clue.text: Grant prisons flexibility for family ties?

indicators.note: Flexibility is the readiness to bend into another shape, and letters given that are not going to stay in the order they came in.

blocks.note: twelve letters across the two words, every one of them reordered

explanation.surface: The jails are being allowed a little room to bend their own rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' reads as the verb of a policy announcement and is raw material instead, which leaves the mild 'flexibility' carrying the whole instruction. A child who cannot leave home is said to be tied to its mother's apron strings.
explanation.definitionFit: family ties → APRON STRINGS: the idiom for the hold a mother keeps on a grown child, the family bond named by the thing it is pictured as.

clue.text: Associate with fool, but not initially

indicators.note: But not cancels whatever is named after it, so the letter picked out there never reaches the grid.

blocks.note: wally is British slang for a fool, the mild insult for someone behaving like an idiot
the letter that word for a fool starts with

explanation.surface: Taking up with an idiot, though not from the very beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' reads as a remark about timing and is counting letters. Wally has meant a fool in Britain since the 1960s, and it is the only word the clue gives you to work on.
explanation.definitionFit: Associate → ALLY: to ally with a country or a cause is to take its side, which is what associating with someone amounts to.

clue.text: Clearly sound touring arrangement

indicators.note: An arrangement is a fresh setting-out of what you already have, so these letters are put in some other order.

blocks.note: seven letters of the one word, all of them reordered

explanation.surface: The plan for a tour looks thoroughly sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' wants to be the adjective of 'a sound arrangement', a sensible plan, and it is the verb: bells and alarms and voices do it.
explanation.definitionFit: Clearly sound → RING OUT: a bell or a shout that rings out is heard plainly over everything around it.

clue.text: Enquires about features

blocks.note: to enquire about something is to go poking round in it, the verb used of a dog or a detective
the features of a face are the parts that stand out on it, and one stands out further than the rest

explanation.surface: Somebody is asking questions about another person's looks.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing marks the join: the three words run on as one phrase and are two definitions laid end to end. 'Enquires' is third person singular, which is what makes the noun plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Enquires about → NOSES, as in noses about a subject, prying into it; features → NOSES, the nose being the feature that sticks out of a face.

clue.text: The empty vessel around a brewing container

indicators.note: An empty word has had its insides taken out, so only the letters at either end of it are left.
Around means encircling, so what is named next goes inside the pieces already assembled rather than after them.

blocks.note: the outer pair of the three-letter word, its middle letter gone
the article as it stands, a single letter
a pot is a vessel for holding liquid

explanation.surface: An empty jug standing round something with a drink fermenting in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The empty vessel' reads as one phrase about crockery, and 'empty' is an instruction aimed at the word 'The' alone. The brewing turns out to be tea rather than beer.
explanation.definitionFit: brewing container → TEAPOT: the pot the leaves are brewed in, which is the brewing vessel of any British kitchen.

clue.text: I turned round to poke my nose in

indicators.note: Something sent round is moved about from where it was standing, so these letters take up other positions.

blocks.note: seven letters, the one-letter pronoun included, put into another order

explanation.surface: Someone spins round and interferes in what is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I turned round' is one movement in the picture and splits in the wordplay, the first two words supplying letters and the third telling you what to do with them. The definition is the whole idiom for meddling.
explanation.definitionFit: poke my nose in → INTRUDE: to push into a room or a conversation nobody invited you into, which is what poking your nose in does.

clue.text: Some agree Ruth is a feminist

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it taken just as it comes, so the letters wanted sit in a run inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: the run begins inside the first word and finishes on the capital of the second

explanation.surface: Opinion is divided over whether Ruth counts as a feminist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some agree' is how you report a split of opinion, and it is the instruction to take part of what comes next. Germaine Greer is the Australian critic whose The Female Eunuch made her a household name in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: a feminist → GREER: Germaine Greer, the writer of The Female Eunuch and one of the movement's best-known voices, so the definition names her by category.

clue.text: Casual, not initially, to accept us, it's the norm

definitions.note: The answer is an adverbial phrase and 'the norm' is a noun, so it is not a straight swap; the setter's 'it's' carries the equation, as usual meaning as the norm has it.

indicators.note: Not takes away the thing named beside it, so the letter picked out there is left out of what is written.
To accept something is to take it in, so the letters named next go inside the word rather than after it.

blocks.note: the whole word to start from, before anything is taken off it
the letter that word begins with, the one that comes off
the pronoun as it stands, two letters to go inside what is left

explanation.surface: Someone stiff at first comes round to us in the end, the way they always do.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make it read as a character sketch, so 'not initially' sounds like a comment on timing while it is counting letters. What is left of 'casual' then opens up to take the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: the norm → AS USUAL: when something happens as usual it happens the way it always has, which is to say as the norm.

clue.text: Chain connections needed for wildcat, we hear

indicators.note: We hear points at the sound of a word rather than its spelling, so what goes in the grid is written the way that word is said.

blocks.note: the lynx is the tuft-eared wildcat of northern forests, and said aloud its name comes out spelt this other way

explanation.surface: The chain you would need to hold a wildcat.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue moves a letter: the entire step is a pronunciation, and the two spellings share no more than their sound. A lynx is the short-tailed wildcat of the northern forests.
explanation.definitionFit: Chain connections → LINKS: the individual rings that hook into one another and so make up a chain.

clue.text: Being without creative subject is naive

blocks.note: art is the creative subject on a school timetable
to go without some of a thing is to have less of it, and as a word ending -less means exactly without

explanation.surface: Living with no creative subject in your life is a naive way to go on.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is the sense of the answer: artless does not mean lacking talent, it means lacking guile, so the definition really is 'naive'. 'Creative subject' meanwhile is a class on a timetable and three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: naive → ARTLESS: artless means without cunning or calculation, the open and unstudied manner a naive person has.

clue.text: Somehow devours horse for starters!

indicators.note: Somehow says the letters end up in some order or other, and not the one they were handed over in.

blocks.note: twelve letters across the two words, every one of them reordered

explanation.surface: Somebody gets through a whole horse before the main course arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For starters' is the everyday phrase for 'to begin with', which is how the definition hides inside the joke about eating a horse. The French is literally 'outside the work' — outside the main business of the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: starters → HORS D'OEUVRES: the small dishes brought before the main course, which is what a starter is on a British menu.

clue.text: Drop fruit that has come across

blocks.note: the stone fruit, four letters
to come across someone is to meet them, and after 'has' the verb takes this form

explanation.surface: Let go of the fruit that somebody has just handed over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop' opens the clue as an order and is the definition instead — the fall a temperature or a share price makes. 'Come across' is wanted in its meeting sense, not the handing-over one the surface asks for.
explanation.definitionFit: Drop → PLUMMET: to plummet is to fall fast and far, the sudden drop a price or a bird makes.

clue.text: Fresh title right for rubbish!

indicators.note: Something fresh has been made over anew, so the letters are set out in a new order rather than the one given.

blocks.note: five letters of the word, to be reordered along with the letter below
r = right, as on a map or in a stage direction

explanation.surface: A new headline turns out to be exactly right for rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh title' reads as a publisher's new book and is the raw material, while 'right' is an abbreviation rather than an opinion. Litter is rubbish in its scattered form, dropped rather than thrown away.
explanation.definitionFit: rubbish → LITTER: the wrappers and papers left lying about a street or a park, which is rubbish where it should not be.

clue.text: Part of East to allow chaps in

indicators.note: In puts the piece named beside it within another word rather than alongside it.

blocks.note: e = east, the compass point
to let someone do something is to allow it, and the word opens up before its last letter
chaps is the informal British word for men

explanation.surface: A region of the East is letting men in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' is the hidden-word setter's standard phrase, so it invites a search through the rest for a buried run; the definition is 'Part' on its own and 'East' is a single letter of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Part → ELEMENT: an element of a plan or an argument is one of the parts it breaks down into.

clue.text: Design of a red hat

indicators.note: To design something is to lay it out afresh, so the letters beside the word are given a new arrangement.

blocks.note: six letters across three small words, all of them reordered

explanation.surface: The pattern of a red hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one noun phrase out of a milliner's catalogue, so it looks like a definition with nothing attached; 'Design' is the verb doing the work. A fedora is the soft felt hat with a creased crown and a pinched front.
explanation.definitionFit: hat → FEDORA: one particular soft felt hat standing for the category, the definition naming the kind of thing it is.

clue.text: US city or country given nothing

blocks.note: the conjunction taken at face value, its own two letters
a country is a land
o = nothing, the zero written as a letter

explanation.surface: A choice between a city and a country, with nothing offered on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like the join between two alternatives and is quietly two letters of the answer, which is what makes the opening of the wordplay invisible. Orlando is the city in central Florida that the theme parks grew around.
explanation.definitionFit: US city → ORLANDO: the Florida city best known for the resorts built beside it, one city standing for the category.

clue.text: Story about abstainer’s gossip

indicators.note: About means round the outside of a thing, so one piece is wrapped round the other instead of following it.

blocks.note: a story is a tale, and the word opens up after its first two letters
tt = teetotal, the two letters a form uses for someone who takes no drink

explanation.surface: A story going round about a man who never touches a drop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Story about' is already what gossip sounds like, which hides the fact that 'about' is placing one piece inside another. TT for teetotal is the only abbreviation in play here.
explanation.definitionFit: gossip → TATTLE: to tattle is to let other people's business out in idle talk, which is gossiping.

clue.text: Boy without a gal, one struggling artist

indicators.note: A boy without something has had it taken off him, so the letter named next is gone from the word before it.
Something struggling is thrashing about and holding no shape, so those letters come out in another order.

blocks.note: Michael is a boy's name, seven letters to start from
the article is one letter, and it is the one that comes out
the informal word for a girl and the number word beside it, six letters put into another order

explanation.surface: A boy with no girlfriend, scraping a living from his painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One struggling artist' is exactly how the garret painter is always described, so the cliché swallows the instruction whole. Michelangelo struggled at nothing: popes queued for him.
explanation.definitionFit: artist → MICHELANGELO: the Florentine sculptor and painter of the Sistine ceiling, one artist standing for the category.

clue.text: Go up cold leg, possibly

indicators.note: Possibly marks the word before it as only one example of something wider, so it is the general word the letters come from.

blocks.note: c = cold, the letter on a tap
a leg is one of the body's limbs, which is the wider word wanted

explanation.surface: Working your way up somebody's cold leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' runs the example trick backwards: the clue names a leg and asks for the general word a leg belongs under. C for cold is the marking on the tap, one of the commonest single letters in the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Go up → CLIMB: to climb a hill or a ladder is to go up it, the same verb used the same way.

clue.text: Opening at front of gangway to put cargo on

indicators.note: The front of a word is where it starts, so only its opening letter is being asked for.

blocks.note: the letter this word starts with
to lade a ship is to load cargo into it, the old verb still alive in 'laden' and 'bill of lading'

explanation.surface: A gap at the top of the gangway where freight goes aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' sounds like a hatch in the side of a ship, which keeps the whole clue down at the quayside; it is a clearing in a wood. Lade survives in English mostly through 'laden'.
explanation.definitionFit: Opening → GLADE: a glade is the open space where the trees stop, an opening in the middle of a wood.

clue.text: Seeing things

blocks.note: read as a verb and its object, this is what you say about somebody imagining what is not there
read as a description of a pair of objects, it names the things whose job is seeing

explanation.surface: Somebody is hallucinating.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, and the whole clue turns on which of them is the noun. Take 'things' as the noun and 'seeing' as what they are for, and the pair in your head answer to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeing things → EYES: the things a person sees with, the phrase read as naming the organs rather than the hallucination.

clue.text: Happening to carry ID to appear obvious

indicators.note: To carry something is to have it on you as you go, so the piece named next travels inside the other rather than after it.

blocks.note: a happening is an event, and the word opens up after its first two letters
the two capitals are taken as they stand, the everyday short form printed on a card

explanation.surface: Someone who happens to have their identification on them so as to look above board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happening to carry' is exactly how you would describe a coincidence, and both halves of it are instructions. ID converts to nothing: those letters are already printed in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: obvious → EVIDENT: what is evident is plain to anyone looking, without needing to be pointed out.

clue.text: Pester to find the 'A' of 'AD' – year, in short

indicators.note: In short asks for the shortened form of the word beside it instead of its full spelling.

blocks.note: AD stands for Anno Domini, so the A in it is short for the Latin anno, 'in the year'
y = year, the usual short form in a date or a guarantee

explanation.surface: Nagging away at what the letters of a date actually stand for.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is taking 'the A of AD' for a single letter. It is an abbreviation inside an abbreviation: the A is standing in for a whole Latin word, and that word is four of the five letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: Pester → ANNOY: to keep at somebody until they are annoyed is what pestering is, and both are transitive verbs for the same nuisance.

clue.text: Overhauled super booster is out of control

indicators.note: To overhaul a machine is to strip it down and put it back together, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: twelve letters across the two words, put into another order

explanation.surface: A rocket booster that has been rebuilt and is now running away with itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overhauled super booster' is workshop language, so the two words read as hardware rather than as raw letters. Obstreperous is noisy resistance — the word for a child who will not be quietened.
explanation.definitionFit: out of control → OBSTREPEROUS: someone obstreperous is noisily unruly and past managing, which is what being out of control looks like in a person.
